s1.syndrome_frame: Acute coronary syndrome with precordial chest pain radiating to the left arm
salient_findings: Severe precordial chest pain radiating to the left arm
ST-segment elevation and depression on ECG
key_facts: Patient is a man in his 50s
Presented with 1 hour of acute, severe precordial chest pain
Chest pain radiated to the left arm
Accompanied by sweating and nausea
Had similar chest pain at rest 6 hours prior that resolved spontaneously
Medical history of hypertension treated with reserpine
Vital signs: blood pressure 170/109 mm Hg, heart rate 87 beats per minute
Initial serum troponin I level: 1.159 ng/mL
ECG showed upsloping ST-segment depression and ST-segment elevation
Coronary angiography revealed 95% stenosis of the proximal left anterior descending artery
Echocardiography showed hypomotility in the anterior wall and left ventricular ejection fraction: 57%

raw.rationale: The patient's presentation with acute, severe precordial chest pain radiating to the left arm, accompanied by sweating and nausea, along with elevated serum troponin I level and ECG changes, is consistent with acute myocardial infarction. The coronary angiography revealing 95% stenosis of the proximal left anterior descending artery and echocardiography showing hypomotility in the anterior wall further support this diagnosis.

rejected.label: Unstable angina
rejected.why: The patient's elevated troponin level and ECG changes indicate myocardial damage, which is not typical of unstable angina

rejected.label: Atherosclerotic coronary artery disease
rejected.why: While the patient has atherosclerotic disease, this diagnosis does not specifically explain the acute presentation

rejected.label: Variant angina
rejected.why: The patient's symptoms and ECG changes do not suggest variant angina, which typically presents with chest pain at rest and transient ST-segment elevation

rejected.label: Coronary artery spasm
rejected.why: The patient's coronary angiography showed significant stenosis, making coronary artery spasm less likely as the primary cause of symptoms

gold: Acute myocardial infarction due to critical stenosis of the proximal left anterior descending artery, presenting with de Winter ECG pattern evolving to Wellens syndrome
